The tatto/tato hot attestations agree with Turner’s Kohistani tato and Guresi tattu under tapta. Single versus double t is preserved as a source variant; neither unrelated kuro nor the separately elicited chat response is merged.

The lōlo red attestation matches Turner’s Gilgit lōlyu/Lorimer loilo under *lohila. This preserves the liquid-bearing red family rather than assigning it to lohita solely by meaning; the simplified vowel/glide transcription remains a review point. Rajapurohit gives lōlo for both red (item 1358) and vermilion (item 1366), supporting a colour-based reading of the merged response. The entry does not establish a distinct word for the pigment substance, so that material sense is not independently asserted.

The bāṛo big attestations agree with Turner’s Shina boṛu/baṛu under vaḍra. The addendum instead analyzes the wider formation as extracted from MIA demonstrative size expressions, so the link identifies the documented family without claiming an undisputed inherited Sanskrit stem.

CDIAL 8416 paútra explicitly records Shina pōc̣ṷ grandson; its full entry and addendum contain no separate Shina subsection or borrowing qualification. Degener independently gives póoc̣o Enkel with T. 8416. The Schmidt, Rajapurohit and HKAT forms preserve the same long-vowel and affricate stem. HKAT uses it for both son’s son and daughter’s son, an extension of the narrower Old Indo-Aryan relationship.

CDIAL 8417 pautrī explicitly records Shina pōc̣i̯ granddaughter; this feminine head is distinct from masculine 8416. Degener confirms póoc̣i Enkelin with T. 8417. The listed forms agree in the feminine ending and long root vowel, with HKAT extending the relationship to daughter’s daughter as well as son’s daughter.

CDIAL 12753 śváśura explicitly gives Shina Gilgit šaiŭr, Gurezi šāir and Palesi šēr father-in-law. The long-vowel and diphthongal modern forms match this attested dialect range; HKAT’s final vowel is retained. The source includes both wife’s and husband’s father within the inherited meaning, and its borrowing comments concern other languages, not these Shina forms.

Schmidt’s jamacōé son-in-law is provisionally compared with the explicit Shina affricate-stem forms under CDIAL 5198 subsection 2 *jāmātra-. Unlike the clearer modern attestations, this transcription lacks the retroflex diacritic and has an additional ending. The kinship meaning and stem support the family comparison, but the source spelling and morphology require review.

Schmidt’s nuʦ daughter-in-law is provisionally compared with the explicit Shina nuṣ/nūṣ under CDIAL 13801 snuṣā. Its final alveolar affricate transcription differs from the expected retroflex fricative, so the otherwise close form and exact kinship meaning do not establish an unqualified sound correspondence. This record requires a transcription check.

CDIAL 5145 jára subsection 1 explicitly records Shina jaru old with feminine jeri; the distinct jaratha subsection is not needed. Degener independently cites T. 5145 for ǰáro alt. The Rajapurohit forms agree in the jar- stem and masculine ending, with the second record’s marked long ā retained as a transcription review point. Schmidt Drasi járu old (person) adds the explicitly attested u-ending and the human sense already represented by Turner’s Shina adjective.

Degener’s primary glossary explicitly analyzes sam well as probably from sāma, referring to Turner 13346 and attributing the suggestion to Buddruss. The full Turner entry groups sāmaka even/level and sāma likeness/sameness; it does not itself cite Shina. This is therefore a tentative semantic development from even/equal to well/good, supported by Degener’s qualified proposal rather than a direct Turner attestation. The head record represents that grouped entry; no unexplained -ka reflex is asserted. The Backstrom/Schmidt good attestations and the well attestation share sam, but their grammatical gloss differences are preserved.

Addendum 14204 redirects to canonical 163 in the graph; 163 alone lacks the Shina citation, so the addendum is the evidential source. Schmidt–Kaul p. 270, Table 2 items 149 and 149a, independently confirms Gilgiti éji for sheep/ewe; its affricate and final i differ from Turner’s ež and remain explicit comparison points.

Schmidt and Kaul list Gurezi and Drasi daṣ grapes among Kashmiri loans (2008, pp. 245–246). Note 21 explains that Gurezi has taken the Kashmiri initial consonant and vowel while retaining retraction in the final consonant, so this is contact-influenced adaptation rather than an unchanged copy. CDIAL 6628 explicitly gives Kashmiri dach, dative dachi; its blank-gloss dach record is the base donor despite a misplaced parsed dat tag. The palatal daś/dáśe records and dáṣṭom are excluded here.

CDIAL 5779 explicitly marks Kashmiri trām copper as the donor of Gilgiti and Gurezi trām; Schmidt and Kaul independently list Gurezi trām under Kashmiri loans (2008, p. 245, example 5). The Gurezi survey record agrees in form and meaning; the proposed parent is the attested Kashmiri word, preserving the immediate borrowing step.

CDIAL 7627 includes Shina phac̣āli wing under pakṣa wing/feather, alongside Kho. poc̣(h) feather and Shina phΛčó tail. Kohistani pac̣háali feather fits this extended Shina formation with aspiration on the affricate rather than the initial stop; the wing/feather sense shift and placement of aspiration are retained as qualifications. This is a historical family assignment, not a claim that the modern suffix has been independently analysed.

CDIAL 11439 vasantá spring season explicitly gives Gurezi băzōnṷ and Jijali bazṓn beside Gilgiti băzōdṷ. Schmidt’s Astori bazō̌nu spring belongs to the n-bearing Shina set, preserving the dialect attribution and pitch notation rather than conflating it with the Gilgiti d-form. Rajapurohit Dras bazṓno adds the same n-bearing seasonal noun with final o rather than u.

CDIAL 5912 explicitly places Kohistani ic̣īzi/ic̣īẓi day after tomorrow under the more specific reconstruction *ātr̥tīyam, whose own entry 1130 gives Shina ic̣ī and cross-refers back. Astori c̣ī̌ẓi matches the fuller zi-ending series with loss of initial i; the specific temporal formation is selected rather than the bare ordinal third. The internal history of the zi ending is not separately asserted.

CDIAL 10442 branch 1 yavyā stream explicitly gives Shina yap irrigation channel, genitive yabai. Rajapurohit pp. 103–104, items 808 and 839, lists yap for a small canal/furrow and contrasts īl for a big canal; the merged Dras yap record agrees with the smaller irrigation-channel sense.

CDIAL 14000 halá plough explicitly records Shina hal. The merged Schmidt and Rajapurohit Dras records all denote the implement; Rajapurohit items 892 and 2541 both give hʌl, distinct from the verbal plough response banthyōno in item 2235.

CDIAL 12081 explicitly gives Kohistani bich scorpion in the vr̥ścika family, tentatively through *vr̥ści. The Gurezi and Drasi Schmidt bic attestations retain the same short form and meaning but lack written aspiration. Both the aspiration difference and Turner’s tentative shorter intermediate are retained; the nearby Kashmiri byuc is itself marked as an Indo-Aryan loan and is not assumed to be the Shina donor.

CDIAL 13929 *svāpra sleep explicitly gives Gilgiti sā̃c̣u dream beside Gurezi sāc̣u and Kohistani sāṣu. Schmidt Drasi sā̃c̣o agrees specifically with the nasalized retroflex-affricate form, preserving the Dras source attribution and final o notation.

CDIAL 3735 kṣetra field directly attests Shina c̣ec̣, with retroflex affricates corresponding to the two ancient clusters. Schmidt Drasi c̣hēc̣ has the same field meaning and stem shape, with aspiration and vowel length explicitly retained as dialectal or transcription differences. The dictionary’s Shina-to-Domaaki arrow is not a claim of borrowing into Shina.

CDIAL 4689 carā moving explicitly compares Shina čar green growing or cut grass, matching Schmidt–Kaul p. 271, Table 2 item 161 Gilgiti car grass/fodder. The proposed semantic bridge through grazing is Turner’s question-marked inference, so the exact modern match supports this as a difficult proposal rather than establishing the deeper semantic development.

CDIAL 11439 vasantá explicitly records Shina bazōdu spring alongside bazōnu. Schmidt and Kaul p. 267 item 108 place bazōdo in Kohistani; the same d-bearing form is supported even though Turner labels his older attestation Gilgit, so the later source’s dialect assignment and final o are preserved.
Turner explicitly gives Brokskat grī neck under grīvā, beside Shina grĩ dewlap/collar. Both the Brokskat form and its specific anatomical sense are directly attested.

The Brokskat kani forms agree with the kaṇṇa/kan ear family documented by Turner, including Shina kon with plural koṇi. The nasal stem distinguishes this from unrelated words for the side of the head.
Brokskat aʦ̣ʰī and LSI aʦʰī have the affricate and final vowel of Turner’s Shina ac̣hī eye under akṣi. Source differences in retroflex notation are retained.
Turner records Shina hat/hath hand under hasta; Brokskat hat and LSI hātʰ share the reduced st cluster. Aspiration and vowel length vary between the two source notations.
The Brokskat dāni tooth stem matches Turner’s Shina don, plural dōnye, and neighboring dān reflexes of danta. The dental nasal outcome and dental meaning support the comparison.

Turner places Shina goṭ house under goṣṭha, subsection 1. Brokskat gōṭ retains the stop, so it fits this branch rather than the competing ghōṣa account for stopless goṣ; LSI does not mark retroflexion.
Brokskat ṣiŋ horn agrees with Turner’s Shina ṣiṅ and the wider Dardic ṣiṅ family. The retroflex initial is the diagnostic outcome of the śr cluster in śṛṅga.
Brokskat mōs flesh agrees with Shina mos/mōs and Kalasha mos under māṃsa. Loss of the medial nasal as a separate consonant is already represented among these comparanda.
Turner explicitly gives Shina ūar belly from udara through the uara type. Brokskat vor and LSI ūar fit contraction and development of an initial glide in this same family.
Brokskat ṣiṣ and LSI śiś head match Turner’s Shina ṣiṣ and Dardic cognates under śīrṣa. This selects the ṣ-final head formation, rather than linking indiscriminately to śiras.
Turner gives Shina krom and Kalasha krum work under karman, with the metathesized kr- also represented in Aśokan kramaṃ. Brokskat krom preserves that diagnostic cluster.
Brokskat rāt night agrees with Shina rāti and Kalasha rat in Turner’s rātrī family. The lost medial r and final vowel are represented in the comparative evidence.
Brokskat hal plough matches Shina hal and widespread Dardic hal reflexes of hala. There is no extra formative requiring a derived or compound link.
Brokskat kōt wood is comparable to Shina kāṭ and the kāṣṭha family. Vowel quality and unmarked retroflexion in this source need review, so the inherited assignment remains provisional.

Brokskat nus daughter-in-law matches Shina nuṣ and Pashai-related nasal/sibilant reflexes in the snuṣā article. The source writes a plain s; this transcription distinction is retained. Batalik nyś son’s wife supports the daughter-in-law comparison; its front vowel and palatal sibilant are preserved alongside Schmidt nus.

Brokskat pōʦ̣o grandson matches Turner’s Shina pōc̣u under pautra. The affricate outcome of tr and masculine final vowel distinguish it from the separately listed feminine pautrī. Batalik pōṭo covers both son’s son and daughter’s son. The ṭ versus ʦ̣ correspondence between sources remains a phonetic qualification.

Brokskat mūmo mother’s brother agrees with Shina māmu in the māma family. Turner identifies a nursery formation, so this proposes family continuity without treating the repeated syllables as decisive proof of remote inheritance. Batalik mūmo also labels father’s sister’s husband, an affinal extension preserved exactly as recorded.

Brokskat mus/myś person agrees with shortened Shina muša in Turner’s manuṣya article. Turner explicitly notes collision with puruṣa and shortening in address terms; retain that limitation rather than claiming an uncomplicated sound-by-sound descent.

Turner places Shina sūri in all dialects under subsection 3 sūriya, distinct from the contracted sūrya branch. Brokskat sari and LSI syrī preserve the medial r and final vowel, with differing vowel notation.

Brokskat śvā points to the śvan paradigm with nominative śvā, rather than the śuna branch proposed for Gilgit śū. LSI śyā and plural śyēō are grouped as source variants; their glide correspondence requires review.

Brokskat panni leaf fits the nasal parṇa > paṇṇa/pan family, not the stop-bearing pattra family of Gilgit paṭu. Compare Turner’s Kashmiri pan; the final -i and possible contact route leave the inherited analysis provisional.

Brokskat guli finger retains l, favoring aṅguli subsection 1 over the *aṅgūḍi branch of Shina agui. Initial reduction and the possibility of a regional loan need review; the compound thumb response is excluded.
Brokskat ek/ēk one retains k, matching Turner’s strengthened *ekka branch, subsection 2. The unstrengthened eka branch has the contrasting loss of k in several northwestern languages.
Brokskat dave and dy two fit the dva paradigm, which includes duve and reduced du/di outcomes. The longer and shorter forms are ordinary numeral variants, not separate derivations.
Brokskat trā three agrees especially with Dameli trā and the long-vowel *trāyaḥ branch, subsection 2. This differs from the short-vowel trayaḥ branch selected for Gilgit ce.
Brokskat cōr/corr four fits the caura/cōra outcomes of accusative caturaḥ, subsection 3, beside Dameli čōr and Kashmiri ċōr. It should not automatically inherit Gilgit čār’s catvāri subsection.
LSI pũś five agrees with Turner’s Shina poš/poṃš under pañca. The Schmidt spelling pods is retained as a questionable source variant requiring transcription review.
Brokskat sā/śā six fits the simple ṣaṭ branch, subsection 1, including Shina ṣa. It lacks the labial element distinguishing Turner’s *ṣuvaṭ branch.
Brokskat sat/sāt seven matches Shina sat and the widespread satta-type reduction of sapta. Both attestations preserve the inherited numeral stem.
Brokskat ãṣ eight closely matches Turner’s Gilgit nasalized aṣ outcome of aṣṭā. The unusual LSI ažrt spelling is left for transcription review rather than silently normalized.

Brokskat nur and LSI ny nine are tentatively compared with the nava numeral family, including northwestern nu/nū outcomes. The r in the Schmidt form is unexplained; neither record is merged with the homonymous adjective new.
Brokskat dās/dāś ten retains the sibilant of daśa, as do Dameli daš and many neighboring forms. This is the numeral itself, not the homonymous day/give response.

Brokskat biẓā/bižā twenty is compared with viṃśati and northwestern biš/bīši forms. Retained voiced sibilant and final vowel distinguish it from Gilgit bi; the exact development remains a moderate-confidence inference.
Brokskat śo/śō hundred matches śata outcomes such as Kashmiri dialect śōu. The numeral remains separate from the similar adjective white.
Brokskat cūdes fourteen fits Turner’s caturdaśa branch with contracted cod-/cud- comparanda. It lacks the metathesized ctr cluster diagnostic of subsection 2 *catrudaśa.
Brokskat sattōṣ seventeen closely matches Palula sattōš in Turner’s saptadaśa article. The historical numeral is linked as a whole rather than split into modern component words.
Brokskat astoṣ eighteen is comparable to Palula aṣṭōš and neighboring aṣṭāš reflexes of aṣṭādaśa. Plain st/s notation in this source is retained rather than silently replaced with retroflex marks.

Brokskat gō cow and its plural gōā fit the gava family. Turner prefers gava for the Shina gō paradigm over direct descent from the irregular go nominative or accusative; extension to Brokskat is provisional.
Brokskat tāto hot matches Shina tātu and Palula tāto under tapta. Reduction of pt to tt/t is explicit in the Middle Indo-Aryan and regional comparanda.
Brokskat śō white agrees with Shina šeo/šyo and Jijal šɔ in Turner’s śveta article. The adjective is kept separate from śō hundred.
Brokskat kyono black is compared with Shina kiṇu and the northwestern kṛṣṇa family. Its palatal glide and rounded vowel require dialectal explanation, so the comparison is provisional.
Brokskat nyy/nø̄ new is compared with Shina nā/nāwu and the contracted nava adjective family. Front-vowel source notation warrants review; the numeral nine remains a separate etymon.
Brokskat bī seed matches Shina bi and the bīja family, with loss of intervocalic j. This favors the bīja head over the distinct bījya branch with retained or strengthened j.
Brokskat mauzi mouse is closest to Turner’s Shina mūẓi under subsection 2 mūṣika, rather than masculine mūẓu under mūṣa. The source’s vowel notation remains a qualification.
Brokskat śuko dry matches Shina šuku/šūku and Palula šuko under śuṣka. The reduced medial cluster is documented in Middle Indo-Aryan sukka/sukkha.

Brokskat zon snake agrees with Shina žon and the specialized snake meaning of jantu, also independently attested in Niya jaṃdunaṃ. There is no -ra extension requiring the separate derived snake formation.
Brokskat nuto/nutō nose matches Shina notu/natu under nastaka, subsection 2. The final vowel supports this extended stem rather than the bare nasta subsection; exact vowel quality differs by source.

Brokskat lyl blood is compared with Shina lēl in Turner’s *lohila family. Turner explicitly prefers this formation over lohita for the Shina lēl pattern; the Brokskat vowel notation keeps the proposal provisional.

Brokskat dut breast matches Shina dut milk under dugdha; Turner also documents breast/teat senses among reflexes of this family. The metonymic anatomical sense is plausible but needs Brokskat-specific confirmation.

Brokskat pis drink contains the pi- stem represented by Turner’s Shina pioiki/pyōnu and widespread pibati reflexes. The infinitive ending belongs to Brokskat morphology and does not require a new etymon.
Brokskat kxus eat and imperative khā agree with the khā-/kho- stem under khādati, subsection 1. The imperative independently confirms the lexical stem despite the unusual kx notation.
Brokskat uthis stand and imperative uthē have dental th, agreeing with Shina uthōnu and the reformed *utthāti subsection. Do not substitute the retroflex *ut-sthāti branch.
Brokskat hāzis laugh matches the voiced-sibilant stem in Shina hažōnu under hasati, beside Pashai az-. This identifies the laughing verb rather than a noun for laughter.

Brokskat maris kill agrees with Shina marōnu and the regional mār- family under mārayati. The inherited killing stem is kept distinct from the dying paradigm and from later causatives meaning have killed.
Brokskat dāhis burn transitively retains h, matching dahati. Its consonant and transitivity distinguish it from the z-bearing intransitive verb, which reflects the old passive formation.

Brokskat dāzis burn intransitively matches Shina dažōnu under dahyate. The contrast with dāhis burn transitively supports preserving two inherited historical stems, rather than deriving one mechanically from the other.

Brokskat khutis beat and imperative kut fit Shina kuṭyōnu and the kuṭṭayati family, subsection 1. Aspiration and absent retroflex notation in the Brokskat source require review; the imperative supports the short-vowel stem over *koṭṭayati.

Brokskat bāyo/bāyō brother compares with Kashmiri bāyi and Gawri blāya, while LSI žrā resembles the cluster-bearing Dardic branch of bhrātṛ. Their relationship may involve contact or competing dialect forms; the family match does not settle the immediate history. Batalik bayo extends across brother, affinal, step, and cousin categories. These exact-form attestations share a provisional lexical-family analysis; the distinct ẓuẓo and compound responses remain outside it.
Brokskat ṣaṣ mother-in-law agrees closely with Turner’s Shina šaṣ under śvaśrū. This is separate from the svasṛ sister family even when source transcriptions make the forms look similar.
Brokskat ścar father-in-law is tentatively compared with Shina šair/šēr and the śvaśura family. Its c notation is not explained by the comparative forms and must be checked before acceptance.

Brokskat ẓamō son-in-law lacks the tr/retroflex-affricate cluster of Shina žamc̣o. It instead compares with Dameli zāmā and Pashai zōmo in jāmātṛ subsection 1; the vowel pattern remains a dialectal qualification.
Brokskat gi ghee exactly matches Shina gi in Turner’s ghṛta family. This is the reduced ghia-type outcome, not a suffixed form such as ghṛtavant.
Brokskat gās grass/fodder agrees with Dameli gās and Kashmiri gāsa under ghāsa. The pasture-grass sense distinguishes this from grāsa mouthful, although both have food-related meanings.
Brokskat cukro sour matches Palula čukro and Dameli čukra in Turner’s cukra family. The adjective belongs to the first semantic group; no independently promoted subsection is required.
Brokskat tino sharp agrees with Shina tīṇu and neighboring tīṇ/tīn outcomes under tīkṣṇa, subsection 1. There is no r supporting the competing *trīkṣṇa branch.
Brokskat ẓigo long matches Turner’s Shina ẓigu and Maiyan žiga under dīrgha. The retroflex initial and retained g make this more specific than a gloss-only comparison.
Brokskat nīlo green agrees with Shina nīlu and Palula nīlo in the nīla color-adjective family. The blue/green range is already part of the primary comparative evidence.

Brokskat licā nit matches Shina līc̣ and Kalasha lic̣ak in the likṣā family. Its initial l selects the main branch rather than the separate *rikṣā reconstruction in the addenda; unmarked retroflexion remains a transcription qualification.
Turner explicitly records Brokskat ēi under avi sheep. The compiled ēy ewe attestation matches this form and meaning, separately from Brokskat ā she-goat under aja.
Brokskat pon/pun path agrees with Turner’s Shina pon and Kho pon under panthā. The reduced nasal-final stem is directly represented in neighboring cognates.

Brokskat hɨɨ heart is compared with Shina hīu and Maiyan hī in the hṛdaya family. Its strongly reduced vowel sequence requires transcription and dialect review, but the retained h and matching anatomical meaning support the proposed comparison.

Brokskat ʦ̣iṭo bitter matches Turner’s Shina c̣iṭu under tṛṣṭa (CDIAL 5938). The separately recorded tīto remains a distinct source synonym and is held for a Kashmiri-loan investigation; it is no longer proposed as a direct tikta reflex.

Brokskat gip/gib tongue agrees in the medial vowel and final labial with Shina jip/jib under jihvā, subsection 1. All three sources write initial g; its historical relationship to the Shina affricate remains to be established, so this is a provisional comparison.

Brokskat turi/turī/tyri star has final -i, favoring *tārikā, subsection 3, beside Kalasha tāri. The rounded/front-rounded vowel varies between sources, so this is a provisional subsection choice rather than an automatic extension of Gilgit tāro under tāraka.

CDIAL 13776 independently attests Kashmiri ṭhūl egg; the donor vowel length and retroflex notation differ from the shorter dental rendering in the Brokskat record, and the analysis preserves the Kashmiri donor instead of linking directly to sthūla.
